text:
The best pick depends on how you camp. Two review sites I could read agree on the same short list. Prices are the ones the reviews listed, so check them before you buy.

**Best by camping style**

| Your trip | Pick | Capacity | Weight | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phones, lights and a laptop on a weekend | **Anker SOLIX C300** | 288Wh | ~9.3 lb | ~$199 |
| Same, but you want more AC power | **EcoFlow River 3 Plus** | 286Wh (expandable to 572Wh) | ~9.9 lb | ~$269–299 |
| Tightest budget | **Bluetti EB3A** | 268Wh | ~10.1 lb | ~$179 |
| Longer trips, a few days of power for a couple of people | **Anker Solix C1000 Gen 2** | 890Wh | 25.2 lb | $799 list, under $530 on sale |
| Van, overland, or a 12V fridge | **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2** | 1,070Wh | ~23.8 lb | ~$799 |
| Off-grid for days, or a bigger setup | **Jackery Explorer 2000 v2** | 1,710Wh usable | 38.9 lb | $1,499 list, under $900 on Amazon |

**My picks**
- **Most people:** The **Anker Solix C1000 Gen 2** was OutdoorGearLab's "Best Value for Most People." It's easy to carry and has plenty of AC ports. Its fan is loud.
- **Light tent camping:** The **EcoFlow River 3 Plus** has double the AC output of the Jackery 300 Plus, charges fast, and has a useful app. The **Anker SOLIX C300** has a built-in lantern and a 5-year warranty. Buy the version with AC outlets, not the DC-only variant.
- **Cheapest:** The **Bluetti EB3A** is the cheapest battery here that uses long-lasting LiFePO4 cells. Its app is basic.
- **Longest off-grid stays:** The **Jackery Explorer 2000 v2** has long runtime and 2,200W output, and it's easy to add solar. It's heavy and can't be expanded.

I'd skip the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 for camping. It weighs 114 lb and suits home backup better.

**Buying links**
I couldn't confirm direct store links for these, so I'm linking the guides I used. Each lists the models, and you can buy from the brands' official sites or Amazon.
- [OutdoorGearLab's power station tests](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/topics/camping-and-hiking/best-power-station)
- [PowerStationGearLab's camping guide](https://powerstationgearlab.com/best/best-portable-power-station-for-camping/)

One more result was a coupon page for the Bluetti AC180. It claims code AFF5OFF takes $24.95 off, from $499 to $474.05, at Bluetti's US store ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/lab/V7/bluetti-ac180)). I didn't open that page, and neither review I read covers the AC180. Treat it as an unverified deal, and check the code at checkout.

Tell me your budget and what you'll power, and I can narrow this to one pick. Useful details include a CPAP, a fridge, or how many nights you'll be out.

**Top camping power station picks**

| Model | Capacity | Weight | AC output | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jackery Explorer 300 Plus | 288Wh | ~8.3 lb | 300W | ~$249 |
| EcoFlow River 3 Plus | 286Wh | ~9.9 lb | 600W | ~$269-299 |
| Anker SOLIX C300 | 288Wh | ~9.3 lb | 300W (600W surge) | ~$199 |
| Bluetti EB3A | 268Wh | ~10.1 lb | 600W | ~$179 |
| Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 | 1,070Wh | ~23.8 lb | 1,500W | ~$799 |

**Pros and cons**

1. **Jackery Explorer 300 Plus (best overall):**
   - *Pros:* Lightest of the group, simple interface, LiFePO4 cells, works with a Jackery solar panel.
   - *Cons:* Jackery's U.S. site no longer lists it, having replaced it with the Explorer 300 v2, which has a shorter warranty. Lower AC output than the River 3 Plus.

2. **EcoFlow River 3 Plus (best value):**
   - *Pros:* Double the Jackery's AC output, expandable to 572Wh, fast recharge, useful app.
   - *Cons:* Heavier and a busier interface.

3. **Anker SOLIX C300 (best for long trips):**
   - *Pros:* Built-in retractable lantern, dual USB-C ports, 5-year warranty.
   - *Cons:* Make sure you buy the AC-outlet version, not the AC-less DC variant.

4. **Bluetti EB3A (best budget):**
   - *Pros:* Cheapest LiFePO4 option here, 600W inverter, fast wall recharge.
   - *Cons:* Basic app and less polish overall.

5. **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (best for van/overland):**
   - *Pros:* Enough capacity for a 12V fridge and devices for a day, 1,500W inverter.
   - *Cons:* Much heavier and pricier, so it's overkill for tent camping.
